\chapter{The Seasons Go Native}
\label{ch:jahreszeiten}
\hlchaptermodality{15}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the four German seasons and say which of them German built and which it inherited.}

The months were bought; the year, the time and the seasons were not. Jahr is English year, Zeit is English tide, and Jahreszeit is the two of them stuck together -- year-time -- where English borrowed season from French. Frühling was built inside German out of früh, and Herbst is English harvest: one inherited word that English narrowed to the act of gathering before buying Latin autumn for the season German never stopped naming with it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[das Jahr]{das Jahr — \textquotedblleft{}the year\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-jahr}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Januar} to \emph{Dezember}. Twelve months. There is a word for the whole of that, and it is not from Latin.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: das Jahr}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{das Jahr} — \textquotedblleft{}the year.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Germanic \emph{jēra}, the twin of English \textbf{year}.

Every one of the twelve names inside it was bought from Rome. The container was not, any more than \emph{Monat} was. German bought the labels and kept the measurements.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{j-as-y} — the \emph{j} is English \emph{y}, as in \emph{Januar} and \emph{Juni}: \emph{yaar}.
  \item \texttt{h-silent-lengthening} — the \emph{h} is not pronounced. It \textbf{stretches} the \emph{a} in front of it, which is the job that \emph{h} does inside a German word.
\end{itemize}

So \emph{Jahr} is two letters of sound and two letters of instruction. Written, it looks nothing like \emph{year}; said, it is the same word.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}das Jahr\textquotedblright{} — yaar, long
  \item the English twin — \textquotedblleft{}Jahr, year\textquotedblright{}
  \item what the h is doing — \textquotedblleft{}stretching the a\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}das Jahr.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}the year.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Das Jahr}.) Is the \emph{h} pronounced? (\textbf{No} — it lengthens the \emph{a}.) What is its English twin? (\emph{\textbf{Year}}.) Borrowed or inherited? (\textbf{Inherited} — like \emph{Monat}, unlike every month name.) Next: the second half of a compound you are about to build.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[die Zeit]{die Zeit — \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-zeit}



\begin{quote}
You have a clock and you have an hour. This is the thing they measure.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: die Zeit}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{die Zeit} — \textquotedblleft{}time.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Germanic, through and through, and the twin of an English word you would not guess: \textbf{tide}.

\emph{Tide} once meant a stretch of time, and it still does in the leftovers — \emph{Yuletide}, \emph{eventide}, \emph{in good time}. Then the sea took the word, and English had to borrow \emph{time}'s job out to a different root. German never had that problem and kept \emph{Zeit} for the whole idea.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{z-ts} — German \emph{z} is \textbf{ts}, as it was at the front of \emph{Dezember}.
  \item \texttt{diphthong-ei} — and \emph{ei} is the vowel of English \textbf{eye}.
\end{itemize}

Put them together: \emph{tsite}, rhyming with English \emph{sight}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}die Zeit\textquotedblright{} — tsite
  \item the English leftover — \textquotedblleft{}Yuletide\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three together — \textquotedblleft{}die Uhr, die Stunde, die Zeit\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}die Zeit.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}time.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Die Zeit}.) How does \emph{z} sound? (\textbf{Ts}.) What is its English twin? (\emph{\textbf{Tide}}.) Where does English still use it that way? (\emph{\textbf{Yuletide}}.) Now hold \emph{Jahr} and \emph{Zeit} together — the next word is both of them.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[die Jahreszeit]{die Jahreszeit — \textquotedblleft{}season\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-jahreszeit}



\begin{quote}
Year. Time. Put them together and say what you think it means before reading on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: die Jahreszeit}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{die Jahreszeit} — \textquotedblleft{}season,\textquotedblright{} and literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{year-time}.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\emph{Jahres-} is \emph{Jahr} with the linking \emph{-es-} German puts between the halves of a compound, and \emph{-zeit} is \emph{Zeit}. Nothing is hidden. The plural is \emph{die Jahreszeiten}, and it is the title of this chapter.

\begin{culture}
English does not do this. English has \emph{\textbf{season}}, from French \emph{saison}, from Latin \emph{satio} — \textquotedblleft{}the sowing.\textquotedblright{} A borrowed word, opaque unless somebody explains it, which is what the previous sentence had to do.

German assembled its word out of two it already owned, and the result explains itself to anyone who has the halves. You had the halves two lessons ago.

That is the difference between the two halves of this chapter and the last one. The months arrived as labels. The year, the time and the seasons were already here, and German named them out of stock.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}die Jahreszeit\textquotedblright{}
  \item its two halves — \textquotedblleft{}Jahr, Zeit\textquotedblright{}
  \item what it says — \textquotedblleft{}year-time\textquotedblright{}
  \item the plural — \textquotedblleft{}die Jahreszeiten\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Jahr, Zeit, Jahreszeit.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}season.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Die Jahreszeit}.) What are its halves? (\emph{\textbf{Jahr}} \textbf{and} \emph{\textbf{Zeit}}.) What does it literally say? (\textbf{Year-time}.) Is English \emph{season} built the same way? (\textbf{No} — it is borrowed from French.) Next: the first of the four.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[früh]{früh — \textquotedblleft{}early\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-frueh}



\begin{quote}
One small word first, because the first season is built out of it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: früh}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{früh} — \textquotedblleft{}early.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Not a noun and not capitalised: an adjective, and one you will meet constantly — \emph{früh aufstehen}, to get up early.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{umlaut-ue} — \emph{ü} is a sound English does not have. Say \textbf{ee}. Hold it. Now round your lips as if for \textbf{oo}, and do not let your tongue move. That is \emph{ü}.
  \item \texttt{h-silent-lengthening} — and the \emph{h} is silent again, stretching the vowel, as it did in \emph{Jahr}.
\end{itemize}

\emph{fr-ü-h}: one syllable, the middle held long.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the vowel alone — \textquotedblleft{}ee, then round the lips\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}früh\textquotedblright{}
  \item what the h is doing — \textquotedblleft{}stretching, not sounding\textquotedblright{}
  \item it beside a word with the same trick — \textquotedblleft{}Jahr, früh\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}früh.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}early.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Früh}}.) How do you make \emph{ü}? (\textbf{Say} \emph{ee}, \textbf{then round the lips}.) Is the \emph{h} sounded? (\textbf{No} — it lengthens.) Next: what German calls the early season.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[der Frühling]{der Frühling — \textquotedblleft{}spring\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-fruehling}



\begin{quote}
You have \emph{früh}. Add three letters.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: der Frühling}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{der Frühling} — \textquotedblleft{}spring,\textquotedblright{} and literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the early one}.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The ending \textbf{-ling} takes a quality and makes a thing that has it. \emph{Früh} is early; a \emph{Frühling} is the early one — the year's first \emph{Jahreszeit}.

You will meet \emph{-ling} again elsewhere, and it does the same job every time.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{umlaut-ue} — the same \emph{ü} as in \emph{früh}, unchanged by the ending.
  \item \texttt{ng-cluster} — and \emph{-ling} ends on the \emph{ng} of English \emph{sing}, with no hard \emph{g} after it.
\end{itemize}

Two syllables, and the weight sits on \emph{früh}, the half that carries the meaning.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the small word — \textquotedblleft{}früh\textquotedblright{}
  \item the season — \textquotedblleft{}der Frühling\textquotedblright{}
  \item what it says — \textquotedblleft{}the early one\textquotedblright{}
  \item it with its category — \textquotedblleft{}der Frühling ist eine Jahreszeit\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}früh, Frühling.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}spring.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Der Frühling}.) What is it built from? (\emph{\textbf{Früh}} \textbf{plus} \emph{-ling}.) What does \emph{-ling} do? (\textbf{Makes \textquotedblleft{}the one that is like that\textquotedblright{}}.) Borrowed or built? (\textbf{Built}.) Next: two seasons that need no explaining at all.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[der Sommer]{der Sommer — \textquotedblleft{}summer\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-sommer}



\begin{quote}
After the built one, an inherited one. This is the easiest word in the chapter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: der Sommer}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{der Sommer} — \textquotedblleft{}summer.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

One Germanic word, kept whole by both languages: \emph{Sommer}, \textbf{summer}. The difference between them is the vowel letter and nothing else.

Words survive like this when nobody ever has a reason to replace them, and a hot season is one of those things every generation needs to talk about.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{vowel-o-german} — a short, rounded \emph{o}, steadier than the English vowel.
  \item \texttt{r-final} — and the ending is the soft \emph{r} you have on \emph{Uhr} and \emph{November}.
\end{itemize}

\emph{SOM-mer}, weight on the first.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Sommer\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}Sommer, summer\textquotedblright{}
  \item two seasons in order — \textquotedblleft{}der Frühling, der Sommer\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}der Frühling, der Sommer.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}summer.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Der Sommer}.) Is it borrowed? (\textbf{No} — \textbf{inherited}, like English \emph{summer}.) Say the first two seasons. (\textbf{Der Frühling, der Sommer}.) Next: the one with a surprise in it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[der Herbst]{der Herbst — \textquotedblleft{}autumn\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-herbst}



\begin{quote}
The third season, and the only one whose name you will not recognise at first hearing.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: der Herbst}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{der Herbst} — \textquotedblleft{}autumn,\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}fall.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

It is the \textbf{reaping} season: the stretch of the year when the crop comes in. That meaning is the whole of the word, and the next lesson is about where else you already have it.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{herz-short-e} — a short, open \emph{e}, the vowel of English \emph{bed}, with the German \emph{r} colouring it from behind.
  \item \texttt{st-initial-scht} — the \emph{-st} here is at the \textbf{end}, so it stays a plain \emph{st}, exactly as it did inside \emph{August}.
\end{itemize}

\emph{hairpst}, one syllable, no vowel between the \emph{b} and the \emph{st}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Herbst\textquotedblright{} — one syllable
  \item what it means — \textquotedblleft{}the reaping season\textquotedblright{}
  \item three in order — \textquotedblleft{}der Frühling, der Sommer, der Herbst\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}der Herbst.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}autumn.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Der Herbst}.) How many syllables? (\textbf{One}.) What does the word mean underneath? (\textbf{The reaping season}.) Next: the English word that is the same word.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Herbst und harvest]{Herbst and harvest}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-herbst-harvest}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{Herbst} once more and then say the English word \textbf{harvest}. Those are the same word.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Germanic \emph{harbistaz}, \textquotedblleft{}the reaping season,\textquotedblright{} went into both languages and then each did something different with it.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{what it kept} & \textbf{what it did next} \\
\midrule
German & \emph{Herbst}, the \textbf{season} & nothing — it was enough \\
English & \emph{harvest}, the \textbf{act} & borrowed Latin \emph{autumn} for the season \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English narrowed the inherited word to the \emph{gathering itself} — you harvest a field — and then found it had no word left for the time of year, so it took one from Latin. German never split the meaning and never needed the loan.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
This is the clearest example in the book of something worth knowing: two languages can inherit \textbf{the same word} and end up looking unrelated, without either of them doing anything strange.

Nobody replaced \emph{harvest}. Its meaning drifted a little, a gap opened where the season used to be, and a Latin word was standing nearby. That is how most borrowing happens — not because a language lacks a word, but because one of its words moved.

And it is the last turn of this chapter's argument. The months were bought outright. The seasons were not, and \emph{Herbst} is the one place you can watch the English side buy what German kept.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}Herbst, harvest\textquotedblright{}
  \item what each language kept — \textquotedblleft{}the season; the work\textquotedblright{}
  \item what English had to buy — \textquotedblleft{}autumn, from Latin\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Herbst, harvest — one word, two jobs.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What English word is \emph{Herbst}? (\emph{\textbf{Harvest}}.) What does English use it for now? (\textbf{The act of gathering}.) So what did English borrow, and from where? (\emph{\textbf{Autumn}}, \textbf{from Latin}.) Did German need a loan? (\textbf{No}.) Next: the coldest one, and then a word most Germans never say.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[der Winter]{der Winter — \textquotedblleft{}winter\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-winter}



\begin{quote}
The fourth season, spelled exactly as you would expect, and said exactly as you would not.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: der Winter}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{der Winter} — \textquotedblleft{}winter.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Same six letters as English, same inherited Germanic word, and like \emph{Sommer} it was never worth replacing.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{w-as-v} — German \emph{w} is an English \textbf{v}. The season is \emph{VIN-ter}.
  \item \texttt{i-short} — and the \emph{i} is short and bright.
\end{itemize}

\emph{November} had the mirror of this: a \emph{v} that is said as an \emph{f}. German's \emph{v} and \emph{w} have swapped the jobs an English reader expects of them, and these two words put both halves of the swap on one page.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Winter\textquotedblright{} — VIN-ter
  \item the swap — \textquotedblleft{}w is v, v is f\textquotedblright{}
  \item all four — \textquotedblleft{}der Frühling, der Sommer, der Herbst, der Winter\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}der Winter.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}winter.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Der Winter} — VIN-ter.) How is German \emph{w} said? (\textbf{As a} \emph{v}.) And German \emph{v}? (\textbf{As an} \emph{f}.) How many \emph{Jahreszeiten} have you now? (\textbf{Four}.) Next: a fifth name for a season you already have.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[der Lenz]{der Lenz — \textquotedblleft{}spring,\textquotedblright{} the old word}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-lenz}



\begin{quote}
German has a second word for spring. You will read it far more often than you will hear it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: der Lenz}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{der Lenz} — \textquotedblleft{}spring,\textquotedblright{} in poetry and in set phrases.
\end{quote}

\emph{Frühling} is the word you use. \emph{Lenz} is the word that turns up in songs, in older writing, and in the odd fixed expression. Recognise it; reach for \emph{Frühling}.

It is older than \emph{Frühling}, and it is the twin of English \textbf{Lent} — which was the \emph{spring} season before the Church attached a fast to it. Both go back to a root about the \textbf{lengthening} of the days, which is the one thing a northern spring reliably does.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{z-ts} — the \emph{z} is \textbf{ts}, as in \emph{Zeit} and \emph{Dezember}: \emph{lents}.
  \item \texttt{herz-short-e} — with the short open \emph{e} of \emph{Herbst}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Lenz\textquotedblright{} — lents
  \item the everyday word beside it — \textquotedblleft{}der Frühling\textquotedblright{}
  \item the English twin — \textquotedblleft{}Lent\textquotedblright{}
  \item which one you use — \textquotedblleft{}Frühling\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Frühling, Lenz.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{Lenz} mean? (\textbf{Spring}.) Which word do you use in speech? (\emph{\textbf{Frühling}}.) What is \emph{Lenz}'s English twin? (\emph{\textbf{Lent}}.) What did the root mean? (\textbf{The lengthening of the days}.) Next: the whole year, said through.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — the four, and the seam}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-jahreszeiten}



\begin{quote}
No new words. A year, a time, and the four things they make between them.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the four seasons}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{built from} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\emph{der Frühling} & \emph{früh} + \emph{-ling} & spring \\
\emph{der Sommer} & inherited whole & summer \\
\emph{der Herbst} & inherited whole & autumn \\
\emph{der Winter} & inherited whole & winter \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three of the four are the plain twins of their English words. The fourth was built inside German out of a word you learned one lesson earlier.

Not one of them was borrowed.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Hold the last three chapters together and the seam is exact.

\emph{ The \textbf{months} came from Rome, all twelve, names and calendar together. } The \textbf{year}, the \textbf{time}, and the \textbf{seasons} did not. \emph{Jahr}, \emph{Zeit}, \emph{Jahreszeit}, and the four seasons are German's own, and \emph{Frühling} was still being built out of German parts long after the month names had arrived.

\emph{Herbst} is the sharpest place to see it, because there English went the other way: it kept the inherited word for the \textbf{work} and bought \emph{autumn} for the \textbf{season}. Two languages, one starting word, opposite outcomes — and the German one is the one that needed no purchase.

And German kept a spare. \emph{Lenz} is still there for spring, older than \emph{Frühling}, unneeded and unretired.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all four — \textquotedblleft{}der Frühling, der Sommer, der Herbst, der Winter\textquotedblright{}
  \item the category — \textquotedblleft{}die Jahreszeiten\textquotedblright{}
  \item the built one and its part — \textquotedblleft{}Frühling, from früh\textquotedblright{}
  \item the compound and its halves — \textquotedblleft{}Jahreszeit: Jahr, Zeit\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair that split — \textquotedblleft{}Herbst, harvest\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Frühling, Sommer, Herbst, Winter.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name the four seasons. (\textbf{Der Frühling, der Sommer, der Herbst, der Winter}.) Which one was built rather than inherited? (\emph{\textbf{Frühling}}, from \emph{früh}.) Which one is English \emph{harvest}? (\emph{\textbf{Herbst}}.) How many of the four did German borrow? (\textbf{None}.) And how many of the twelve month names? (\textbf{All of them}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
